'''''Amaranthus tuberculatus''''', commonly known as '''roughfruit amaranth''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=AMTU|taxon=Amaranthus tuberculatus|accessdate=7 January 2016}}</ref> '''rough-fruited water-hemp''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> '''tall waterhemp''', or '''common waterhemp''',<ref name="Mizzou-WeedID">{{ cite web | url=http://weedid.missouri.edu/weedinfo.cfm?weed_id=319 | title=Common Waterhemp // Mizzou WeedID }}</ref><ref name="On-Ag">{{ cite web | url=http://www.omafra.gov.on.ca/english/crops/field/weeds/common_waterhemp.htm | title=Waterhemp, Common (Amaranthus Rudis L.) }}</ref> is a species of [[flowering plant]].  It is a summer annual broadleaf with a germination period that lasts several months.<ref name=Gower>{{cite journal|first=Stephen |last=Gower |author2=Chad Lee |title=Tall Waterhemp Management in Corn and Soybeans |publisher=Center for Integrated Plant Systems, Michigan State University |date=November 2001 |url=http://www.pestid.msu.edu/profiles/TallWaterhemp.PDF |accessdate=2025-03-22 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070727005524/http://www.pestid.msu.edu/profiles/TallWaterhemp.PDF |archivedate=2007-07-27 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
Tall waterhemp has been reported as a [[weed]] in 40 of 50 [[U.S. states]].<ref name=plants>{{cite web |url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=AMTU/symposium.shtml |title= ''Amaranthus tuberculatus'' (Moq.) Sauer |work=PLANTS Database|publisher=United States Department of Agriculture | access-date = 2007-12-26}}</ref>

==Morphology==
A distinguishing characteristic of tall waterhemp that sets it apart from similar members of the genus ''[[Amaranthus]]'' is the lack of hair on its [[plant stem|stems]] and [[leaf|leaves]]. This characteristic gives the leaves a bright, glossy appearance. The stem is typically erect and slender, which can be up to three feet long with a color of either green or red.<ref name=Gower/> 
 
Tall waterhemp is a [[dioecious]] plant.  The seedhead branches in the female are numerous, short, and smooth. The male seedhead branches are fewer, longer, and more slender than those of the female.

The species has terminal spike [[inflorescence]]s and very short [[bract]]s with simple to highly branched flowers. Seed produced is reddish to black and less than 1/32 inch in diameter.<ref name=Stritzke>

==Geographic distribution==
Tall waterhemp is native to [[North America]]. It is believed to have originally had a range north of [[Missouri]] and [[Tennessee]] to the [[Great Lakes]].<ref name=fona/>  It is now found in 40 states but is most common in the [[Great Plains]] and [[Great Lakes]] regions.<ref>[http://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Amaranthus%20tuberculatus.png Biota of North America Program 2014 county distribution map]</ref> Tall waterhemp predominantly grows in wet habitats, such as ponds, marshes, lakes, creeks, and other [[riparian]] zones. The plant can grow in a variety of climates, including roadways, railroads and agricultural fields.<ref name=fona/>

==Growth and development==
Tall waterhemp is a [[summer annual]] that produces a large number{{quantify|date=August 2008}} of very small{{quantify|date=August 2008}} seeds. It is considered an [[r-strategist]]. [[Emergence]] can span several months and often occurs later in the season than other annual weeds, allowing the weed to evade typical weed control strategies such as [[herbicide]] application and [[tillage]].<ref name=Gower/>  One study observed 80% emergence not occurring until ten weeks after the initial emergence.<ref>Weekly emergence of waterhemp and giant ragweed in Ames, IA.  2000.  Sandell, Buhler and Hartzler, Iowa State University</ref>  Extreme temperatures have little effect on seed viability.  [[Germination]] occurs typically after soil temperature alternation, as this is required to break seed dormancy.<ref>Leon RG, Knapp AD, Owen MDK (2004) Effect of temperature on the germination of common waterhemp (Amaranthus tuberculatus), giant foxtail (Setaria faberi), and velvetleaf (Abutilon theophrasti). Weed Science: Vol. 52, No. 1 pp. 67–73</ref>  Waterhemp has been found to germinate in a wide range of soil and temperature conditions.<ref name =isu/>  It has been found to germinate 17 years after seed set.<ref>Burnside, O.C., R.G. Wilson, S.Weisberg and K.G. Hubbard. Seed longevity of 41 weed species buried 17 years in eastern and western Nebraska.  Weed Sci.  44:74-86.</ref>

While tall waterhemp cannot [[self-pollination|self-pollinate]], due to having separate male and female plants, it does not require any vectors for pollination.<ref name=isu>{{cite web|url=http://www.weeds.iastate.edu/mgmt/2003/symposium.shtml  |title= Waterhemp - The Perfect Weed? |work=Weed Science|publisher=Iowa State University | accessdate = 2007-12-26 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20061018184807/http://www.weeds.iastate.edu/mgmt/2003/symposium.shtml |archivedate = 2006-10-18}}</ref>  This allows for wind pollination over large distances, generating a large amount of [[genetic diversity]].  Another factor contributing to [[genetic diversity]] is the large amount of seed produced.  Tall waterhemp in competition with [[soybean]] has been reported to produce from between 300,000 and 5,000,000 seeds per plant.<ref name=j>Hartzler, R.G., B.A. Battles and D. Refsell.  2004.  Effect of common waterhemp emergence date on growth and fecundity in ''Glycine max''.  Weed Sci.  52.</ref>  Tall waterhemp also has a rapid growth rate, 50–70% greater than other annual weeds.<ref>Horak, M.J. and T.M. Loughin.  2000.  Growth analysis of four ''Amaranthus'' species.  Weed Sci.  48:347-355.</ref>

==Interspecific hybridization==
Interspecific hybrids of tall waterhemp and ''[[Amaranthus hybridus]]'' have been observed in experimental fields<ref>Trucco, F., M.R. Jeschke, A.L. Rayburn, and P.J. Tranel. 2005. Amaranthus hybrids can be pollinated frequently by ''A. tuberculatus'' under field conditions. Heredity 94:64–70.</ref> but have not been observed in agronomic fields.<ref>Rayburn, A. Lane, McCloskey, R., Tatum, Tatiana C., Bollero, German A., Jeschke, Mark R., Tranel, Patrick J.  Genome Size Analysis of Weedy Amaranthus Species. Crop Sci 2005 45: 2557-2562</ref>

==Agricultural impacts and control==
In [[North America]], tall waterhemp is considered a major weed of agricultural fields and other disturbed habitats.<ref name=fona>{{cite web |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242415651 |title= ''Amaranthus tuberculatus'' |work=Flora of North America Vol. 4 |publisher=www.eFloras.org }}</ref>  The Southern Weed Science Society includes tall waterhemp on their list of weed species.<ref>Southern Weed Science Society. 1998. Weeds of the United States and Canada. CD-ROM. Southern Weed Science Society. Champaign, Illinois</ref>  However, it is not listed on the federal [[noxious weed]] list or any state lists in the [[United States]].<ref name=nox>{{cite web|url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/noxComposite |title=Federal and State Noxious Weeds |work=PLANTS Database |publisher=United States Department of Agriculture |access-date=2007-12-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071222120604/http://plants.usda.gov/java/noxComposite |archive-date=22 December 2007 |url-status=live }}</ref>  In [[Europe]] and other continents where the species has been introduced, naturalization is an infrequent occurrence.<ref name=fona/>

Because of the long germination window for tall waterhemp, a single herbicide application is unlikely to be an effective control strategy.<ref name="I-Will-Take-Action">{{ cite web | url=http://iwilltakeaction.com/weed/common-waterhemp | title=Waterhemp {{pipe}} Take Action }}</ref> [[Michigan State University]] Extension recommends a preemergence application followed by one or more postemergence applications.<ref name=Gower/><ref name="I-Will-Take-Action"/> Some populations of tall waterhemp have been reported resistant to [[acetolactate synthase]] inhibiting (ALS) [[herbicides]]<ref name="I-Will-Take-Action"/> and the [[triazines]],<ref name="I-Will-Take-Action"/> with some individual weeds being resistant to both [[herbicides|herbicide]] groups.<ref name="I-Will-Take-Action"/> Resistance to [[acifluorfen]] and other diphenyl ether herbicides has been reported.<ref name=Gower/><ref name=isu/> Even more alarming is the emergence of waterhemp resistant to the latest generation of herbicides, [[4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase inhibitor|HPPD inhibitors]].<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.thecropsite.com/news/7530/waterhemp-is-first-to-evolve-hppd-resistance | title=Waterhemp is First to Evolve HPPD Resistance }}</ref><ref name="I-Will-Take-Action"/> Furthermore, waterhemp at a site in [[Nebraska]] was found to be resistant to [[2,4-Dichlorophenoxyacetic acid|2,4-D]], a [[phenoxy herbicide]].<ref>{{Cite journal |doi = 10.1614/WS-D-11-00170.1|title = A Waterhemp (Amaranthus tuberculatus) Population Resistant to 2,4-D|journal = Weed Science|volume = 60|issue = 3|pages = 379–384|year = 2012|last1 = Bernards|first1 = Mark L.|last2 = Crespo|first2 = Roberto J.|last3 = Kruger|first3 = Greg R.|last4 = Gaussoin|first4 = Roch|last5 = Tranel|first5 = Patrick J.| bibcode=2012WeedS..60..379B |s2cid = 86730513}}</ref><ref name="I-Will-Take-Action"/>

According to Bob Hartzler of [[Iowa State University]], the most effective control of tall waterhemp is achieved by cultural practices that promote growth of the desired vegetation.<ref name=isu/>
